comments.author: passyourownbutter
comments.body:
Currently using gpt image gen 2.5 to create reference sheet, upload to meshy and generate, remesh to lower faces and vertices, texture with same reference sheet, rig if it's animated, download or bridge import to blender, activate mcp and have astra or opus evaluate and improve the meshy rigging, make test/target pose sheets to validate visually and iterate until acceptable.

Chat with your agents about how to rig and animate appropriately in blender.

Rinse and repeat steps as needed to reach desired results.

I'm just learning this but so far that's where I am.

replies.author: passyourownbutter
replies.body:
I've been very impressed so far with the results of the models, the rigging can be a bit messed up but it's serviceable I think it really depends on the shape/figure and the detail on the texture.

I'm using adaptive remesh with high faces and then I used the auto rig on a character that is technically bipedal but not exactly humanoid and it worked well enough for opus to clean up the rigging and make a decent pose sheet. 

I haven't got to animating that character yet but so far so good. I individually modeled some of its accessories so they are not part of the base mesh and had opus connect it all in blender with a reference image. 

The remesh needs some trial and error depending how low you are going but afaik it's free to remesh so no wasted tokens. 

I just have the lowest paid meshy acct for now.

I did have some issues with textures for the characters back but I realized the left/right/back images were the problem, removed the rear image and left only front left and right and it nailed the rear textures. 

I've also had good success using a multi panel reference sheet in a single image rather than using the multi view with individual images for each view but, your mileage may vary of course.

replies.author: Haster
replies.body: Do you have animation experience? I'm fully open to the idea that it's a skill issue on my part but what you describe is so extremely far from my experience it's a bit impressive. It's entirely possible that if I had just a bit of knowledge myself I'd be able to bridge the gap a bit.

replies.author: passyourownbutter
replies.body:
I don't have modeling or animating experience, I downloaded blender and signed up for meshy just this week. I now wish I did have some though because i wouldn't have to lean on the agents so much and these tools are very cool but.. i think we're all learning as we go for the most part!

I regularly have my agents research the proper workflows, read software manuals, investigate how other people are doing things and develop a method to proceed with based on that when it's something I don't know how to do. 

Is the model you are working on complex or what sort of issues are you having in terms of getting the model to match the reference image?

replies.author: Haster
replies.body:
I've tried so many different ways and they all had different reasons for failing. The problem I had with what you seem to be having some success with is that the model doesn't seem to make a distinction between what should read as rigid and what should read as solid. I've had spears turn into noodles when they swing, shields deform massively when the model runs, that sort of thing. I also have weird problems where the color 'bleeds' for lack of a better word to describe what's going on. the blue of a shirt doesn't follow the line of the garment.

The meshy approach is the one that I have the most hope for since it does make nice set pieces if they don't need to be animated and I think if I learned a bit myself I might be able guide the AI into fixing the other issues.

replies.author: passyourownbutter
replies.body:
So I had some texture issues where I actually gave meshy too many views, I had front left back and right but the detail on the back was messed up because it was trying to turn the left right and back into a cohesive thing but the back image was slightly off. Removing that example from the multi view fixed the back texture for me. 

In terms of solid and soft objects, are you then rendering a model with spear in its hand and shield on its arm? 

I would try stripping it down into pieces. Just the character in T pose or A pose, then just the spear and just the shield. 

If the spear is connected to the wireframe of the character as part of the same mesh, it will deform awkwardly when you move the hands and stuff, but if it's a separate object you can animate the character and then just attach the objects where they go.

Anything that needs its own behaviour or movement I think should be its own rendered object model. 

For instance my character has a hat and a handheld accessory, so I had imagen2.5 spin up reference images for the complete character, the bare character and each of its pieces, a hat, the hats cord and the handheld object, so I ended up getting 4 separate models from meshy and linking them together in blender to match the complete reference image. 

Each reference image was a single image with 4+ views in collage.

replies.author: Haster
replies.body: I tried it both ways, the animations with equipment tacked on were really rough but that might be more fixable than noodle spears. Have you had much luck animating things that aren't living/humanoid things? like a windmill or trees waving in the wind? Not with meshy but with ai.

replies.author: passyourownbutter
replies.body:
Haven't got that far yet personally but my assumption would be that it should be easier to animate something that just spins in place. Again though the wheel/turbine would be a separate piece from the actual windmill.

I'd be interested to know when you have success what worked for you!
